INTRO_KICKER: For brand managers, art directors, and their agencies
INTRO_TITLE: Use Case: Product Launches & Brand Activations
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a brand uses Oddtoe for a product launch or a brand activation, from the first drawing to the object standing in a shop. The worked example is a three-metre replica of the product on a plinth for launch morning, then touring retailers. The same steps apply to a brand character, a mural, a pop-up piece, or a short animation built on the same object.
INTRO_COL2: Every quarter has a product that needs a picture, a social moment, and something for retail. A prop shop will sell you a big bottle. Oddtoe draws it first, and the drawing is the difference between a large object and a picture people send each other. Before this studio I was political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper, and a launch photograph is the same problem as a cartoon: one image, about a second of attention, and no room for a caption. The object gets designed to pass that test.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe handles the first three stages of a launch object: where the idea comes from, how the product gets drawn at ten times its size, and how the finished piece packs up and travels from launch morning to the retailers.
DRAW1_BODY: What is the one picture from launch morning? The product ten times bigger is a start, and a decent one. Better if it is doing something: pouring, opening, lit from inside, wearing the campaign. Oddtoe works out the joke, the feeling, and what the brand needs said before anything gets measured.
DRAW2_BODY: The product drawn flat, front and side, at ten times its size. Then in 3D, so the fabricator gets panels and dimensions and you get a render of the thing on its plinth in the actual foyer. A label that reads at hand size goes wrong at three metres, so type, curves and colour get argued out here. You sign off on paper.
DRAW3_BODY: Launch morning is one day. After that the piece has a year of work to do: the flagship window, a trade show, the retailers who asked for it. So it is designed to come apart, fit through a shop door, go into a road case, and go back together by two people with no tools. Oddtoe sorts that out on the drawing, so the tour does not need a technician.

PANEL_KICKER: What the launch did, and how to count it...
PANEL_TITLE: What a Launch Object Does to Your Numbers
PANEL_INTRO: A three-metre version of the product standing in the foyer at nine in the morning. Nobody has to ask anyone to take a photo. The phones come out on their own. Then come the questions a brand manager gets in the Monday meeting. What did the launch do, and can you show it? Most of it can be counted: coverage, posts, and orders from the shops that had the object, against the ones that did not.
PANEL_ITEM1_TEXT: Trade and consumer press that ran the picture, and how many people each one reaches
PANEL_ITEM2_TEXT: Posts tagged from launch morning and from every retailer stop, against your last launch
PANEL_ITEM3_TEXT: Orders and sales in the shops that had the object, against the shops that did not
PANEL_OUTRO: I like the tracking set up before launch morning, with last launch as the baseline. Oddtoe shares a founder with the Datalabs Agency, a data visualisation studio, so a dashboard that shows whether the launch worked can be part of the job.
CIRCLES_TITLE: 6 IDEAS FOR YOUR NEXT PRODUCT LAUNCH
CIRCLES_SUB: Six jobs a brand hires Oddtoe for in a launch year. Roll over a circle and pick the one your product could carry.
CIRCLES_FOOT: Want one of these for your launch? Send the date and the product. The stunt has a page of its own: publicity stunts.
CIRCLE1_BODY: The bottle, jar, lipstick or headset at three metres, on a plinth, in the foyer on launch morning. Afterwards it goes into a road case and does the flagship window and the trade show, then every retailer who asks. One build, and it gets photographed all year.
CIRCLE2_BODY: A character designed once and drawn properly, so it works on the pack, in a thirty-second animation, and as a costume at the store opening. The same face in all three places, because the same person drew all three.
CIRCLE3_BODY: The product turns up somewhere it should not be, at a size it should not be, for one morning, and leaves before the council can hold a meeting about it. The photograph is the launch. A brand version of the publicity stunt page.
CIRCLE4_BODY: Street art for the launch on a wall the audience already walks past, painted by hand the week before. It stays up for months and gets photographed by people who never clicked on an ad in their lives.
CIRCLE5_BODY: Short animated pieces for social, built on the same character or the same giant object, so the feed and the foyer match. Generative-AI animation makes a whole series of them affordable, drawn in your character’s style instead of stock footage.
CIRCLE6_BODY: A pop-up shop or a press day needs one thing worth standing next to. A built object outside the door, lit after dark, does more for the queue than anything the shopfitters put inside.
WHO_KICKER: Brand managers, product marketing, and their agencies
WHO_COL1: Drinks brands, food and supermarket brands, beauty, fashion, tech and consumer electronics, and the agencies that work for them. A different product in the hand, and the same brief: a launch date, a picture that has to travel, and something for retail. Brand managers own the date and the budget line. They need a picture to show the board before the money is spent, and a number afterwards. Product marketing needs the object to keep working after launch morning: the flagship window, the trade show, the retailers.
WHO_COL2: Art directors at the agency get asked for the idea that is not another billboard. Bring the campaign and I draw what it looks like as an object, at scale, standing where it will stand, so there is a picture to put in front of the client. Agencies can commission on a client’s behalf and keep the client relationship. The quote, the schedule and the progress reports come to you. Oddtoe works to the art director, not around them. For the longer list of things a brand can build, see brand activation ideas.
TIMELINE_TITLE: A LAUNCH, FROM BRIEF TO THE SHOP FLOOR
STEP1_TITLE: Every launch looks like every launch
STEP1_BODY: A hired room, a screen, a countdown, a curtain, and the product on a table looking exactly the size it is. The trade press runs the pack shot they were sent. So before anything gets drawn we settle one question: what does the launch morning photograph show that the pack shot cannot?
STEP1_CRAFT: Editorial judgement, from years of drawing to a deadline
STEP1_CAPTION: Notes on the page, before anything is drawn
STEP2_TITLE: The product, drawn at ten times scale
STEP2_BODY: Front and side, flat, at ten times its size, and then in 3D. At three metres the label is a wall of type and the cap is a table, so the proportions get argued out here, and the brand team sees the thing on its plinth in the actual foyer before it exists. You approve a picture, at the size it will be.
STEP2_CAPTION: Pattern drawings pinned up, with a maquette to check them against
STEP3_TITLE: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker
STEP3_BODY: A three-metre replica is a specialist fabricator’s job, working from my drawings, here or near you. A lighter piece comes out of my own workshop. Either way it has to photograph without glare under shop lighting, come apart into a road case, and go back together by two people with no tools. I check the build against the drawings before it leaves.
STEP4_TITLE: The plinth, the product, and the phones
STEP4_BODY: Delivered the night before, on the plinth by seven, nobody on a headset. The press shot happens with the real product next to its three-metre twin, and everyone in the room takes the same picture and posts it. Two people and a trolley are the whole production.
STEP4_CRAFT: Built to be installed by two people
STEP4_CAPTION: On the launch floor, seams and all
STEP5_BODY: Into the road case, into the flagship window for the month, then the trade show, then the retailers who asked for it. Each stop is another set of photos tagged with the product, and the shops that had it are the ones to compare against the shops that did not.
STEP5_CRAFT: One object, a year of stops
STEP5_CAPTION: Outside a building, doing the same job it did on launch morning
STEP6_TITLE: The brand keeps all of it
STEP6_BODY: First the object, in its road case, ready for next year’s range. The character artwork and the scale drawings, which work on pack, print and screen without redrawing. And the footage from launch morning and every retailer stop, shot by your own crew and by everyone who walked past with a phone.
STEP6_CAPTION: Made once. Still there years later
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_COL1: A product at ten times its size is a cartoon. That is the appeal for me. Exaggeration is what a cartoonist does all day, and a giant bottle on a plinth is the same trick with a budget behind it. The other appeal is that a launch has a deadline nobody can move and an audience that did not come to see art. Work that has to earn its second of attention in a shopping centre is the kind I like making, and it is close to street art, which is where my own work is heading.
WHY_COL2: A brand character is the other reason. Designed properly once, it turns up on the pack, in the animation and in costume, and it is still recognisably the same person. Most brands never get that far because the three jobs go to three suppliers. I like being the one drawing all three. The practical upside for a brand is that the person designing the launch object has a stake in whether the photograph works. I want it to travel for the same reason you do.

WYG_KICKER: The object, the artwork, and the footage afterwards
WYG_TITLE: What Does a Brand Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: The object, the drawings it was built from, and the photos and video from launch morning and every stop after it. All of it is yours to keep, road case included, and it comes out again for the next range. • The object — in this example a three-metre replica of the product on its plinth • The character and scale artwork — the same designs flat, for pack, point of sale, print and social • A road case it packs into and tours in • Photos and video from the launch and each retailer stop, ready for press and for phones
WYG_COL2: The artwork is the part people forget to ask for. Because the object is built from finished drawings, the brand also owns a character or a product illustration that works on a pack, a poster, a shop window and a phone screen without redrawing anything. It can be whatever the launch needs: a giant product, a brand character, a mural, a pop-up piece, or the same character animated for social. They are designed together, so what is on the feed is the same thing as what is in the foyer.
PKG1_BODY: We work out what launch morning needs to look like before we work out what to build. Bring the product, the date, the campaign, and whatever the agency has already drawn.
PKG2_KICKER: Drawn until you can see it
PKG2_BODY: The product at ten times scale, front and side, then in 3D and dropped into a photo of the foyer. You sign off on a picture of the thing, at the size it will be, before a fabricator is booked.
PKG3_BODY: Weight, finish, and how it comes apart. Whether it fits through the flagship door. Freight, customs and quarantine, if it tours. And the launch date, which nobody can move.
PKG4_BODY: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker for the piece: a specialist fabricator for the three-metre replica, my own workshop for lighter work. Finished for shop lighting and made to go back together without a technician.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports, a plan against your launch date, and a retail tour schedule worked out with whoever runs your trade marketing.
CRED_COL1: A launch photograph and a newspaper cartoon do the same job. You get about a second of someone’s attention, and if the picture needs a caption you have already lost them. Oddtoe drew editorial cartoons at college in Delaware, then worked as political cartoonist and chief designer for a Washington DC paper. Years of choosing the one image a story runs with, and watching an editor bin the ones that were too clever. That eye decides what the giant product should be doing on its plinth, and what to leave out.
CRED_COL2: The other half is making. Oddtoe is a prop designer and maker, and offers prop fabrication for the pieces that need a specialist shop. The drawings go out with panel patterns and dimensions a fabricator can build from, and I check the build against them. A prop shop can build the object without the drawing. What I add is the drawing first, then a build checked against it, so the picture is settled before anyone orders material and the object matches the picture when it arrives on launch morning.

FAQ.q: What does this product launch use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of a product launch. It follows one brief - a brand with a launch date and no picture - from the first question through design, fabrication, launch morning, the retail tour, and what the brand still owns afterwards. It uses a three-metre replica of the product as the example, and a brand character, a mural, a pop-up piece or an animated series would follow the same shape.

FAQ.q: How long does a product launch object take?
FAQ.a: Six to eight weeks from brief to launch morning for a lighter built piece from my own workshop. A three-metre replica from a specialist fabricator, or an inflatable, takes longer, because the maker builds it from the drawings; allow [Oddtoe: fill] weeks. Design and approval come first and are the part worth protecting, so the earlier the brief lands, the better the object.

FAQ.q: What does a product launch object cost?
FAQ.a: Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by what the object is, how large, how much structure it needs, what finish the brand wants, and how far it tours. It is costed the same way as any other prop fabrication job. Send the product, the date and the tour plan and you get a quote.

FAQ.q: Can it tour retailers, or be shipped overseas?
FAQ.a: Touring is what it is designed for. The object comes apart into a road case, fits through a shop door, and goes back together by two people with no tools. For overseas, freight and customs get worked through with a freight agent as part of the job, including any treatment or certification the materials need. Often the simpler answer is to have it built near you, working from the drawings.

FAQ.q: What is the difference between a product launch and a brand activation?
FAQ.a: A product launch has a product and a date. A brand activation is the same kind of object without a new product behind it: a pop-up, a festival presence, a stunt for the brand itself. The design and build steps are identical, so this page covers both, and the longer list of formats is on brand activation ideas.

FAQ.q: Can we use it again for the next range?
FAQ.a: Yes, and it should be planned that way. It goes back in its road case after the tour and comes out for the next launch, the next trade show, or the flagship window at Christmas. Used a few times, one build can cost less than hiring something new for each occasion.

FAQ.q: Can you do the animation and the brand character as well?
FAQ.a: Yes, and they are designed together when the brief calls for it: the same character on the pack, in costume, and animated for social, and the same giant object projected on a wall after dark. See generative AI animation for how the animated pieces get made.
Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.
